items.bodyEn: Mishima, the eleventh post town, was where westbound travelers slept after crossing the Hakone pass, so it filled with inns: the 1843 road survey counted seventy-four. The town grew around Mishima Taisha, the chief shrine of Izu, and the Shimoda road branched off here. Hiroshige drew its travelers leaving at dawn, dissolving into grey mist past the shrine's torii.
items.sourceNote: Tōkaidō shukuson taigaichō (1843); Hiroshige, Mishima: Morning Mist (1833–34)

items.bodyEn: Mishima stands where an old lava flow from Fuji ends. Rain and snowmelt sink into the porous rock upstream and surface here as cold, clear springs that feed the Genbei River, which threads between the houses of the old town. Locals call Mishima the city of water, mizu no miyako, and you can still drink from some springs.

The ikenai of 〜てはいけない is the verb iku, to go, in its potential form ikeru, can go, made negative: it won't go, so it won't do. From there it came to mean not allowed and plain bad. In speech ては shrinks to ちゃ and では to じゃ, so you will hear たべちゃいけない more often than the textbook form.
items.sourceNote: Daijisen and Kōjien, entry いけない (行ける + ない)

items.titleEn: Flower or Nose: Hear the Drop
items.bodyEn: Hana means flower and nose; only the pitch tells them apart. In flower, the voice rises on na, then falls on whatever follows: hana-ga with ga low. In nose, the pitch rises on na and stays high: hana-ga with ga high. You need not produce this yet; just notice that the drop, not the vowel, carries the difference.
